variants.name: Akka/Pekko Streams buffers and OverflowStrategy
variants.implementation_notes: The dominant Scala realization is a Reactive Streams engine: Akka/Pekko Streams propagates demand between stages, so a slow sink slows the whole graph, and buffer(n, OverflowStrategy.backpressure|dropHead|dropTail|dropNew|dropBuffer|fail) makes one bounded stage explicit while mapAsync(parallelism) bounds in-flight asynchronous work. The classic queue-and-block structure is replaced by the materializer's queues and the demand protocol; note that every asynchronous operator carries an internal input buffer (default 16, Attributes.inputBuffer(i, m)) which prefetches and therefore hides pressure from time- or rate-driven stages unless it is set to 1. Choose the overflow strategy deliberately - each drop variant loses different elements and only `fail`/`backpressure` preserve all of them.
variants.code_sketch:
val jobs: Source[Job, NotUsed] = inboundJobsConnector()

jobs.buffer(1000, OverflowStrategy.backpressure)     // bounded, slows upstream
    .mapAsync(parallelism = 8)(process)              // bounded in-flight work
    .runWith(Sink.ignore)
// sheds instead (lossy): .buffer(1000, OverflowStrategy.dropHead)
pitfalls: Every .async stage's internal input buffer (default 16) prefetches, so rate/time operators see unexpected values until Attributes.inputBuffer(1, 1) is set.
OverflowStrategy dropHead/dropTail/dropNew/dropBuffer silently discard different elements; only fail and backpressure preserve data.
A source that does not implement demand (a polling connector, a broker subscription) is not slowed by downstream backpressure - those need rate limiting or a bounded queue plus an explicit policy.
Blocking inside a stream stage starves the dispatcher: route blocking calls onto a dedicated dispatcher configured for blocking work, or model them with mapAsync.

variants.name: ZIO Streams pull-based pipelines
variants.idiom_name: ZStream buffer(n) / mapZIOPar(n) with a pulling sink
variants.implementation_notes: ZIO Streams takes the pull route: nothing is computed until the sink pulls an element, so the equivalent of backpressure is structural - the classic queue is replaced by a lazy ZStream pipeline and buffer(n) only decouples two stages through a bounded internal queue. Because every stage is on-demand, operators such as mapZIOPar(n) bound parallelism by construction and there is no strategy to choose for the default case; an unbounded buffer(n) or a Queue.unbounded is again the way to lose the property. Choose this variant when the application is already effect-based and the pipeline is described declaratively rather than wired as a graph of callbacks.
variants.code_sketch:
ZStream.fromIterable(events)
    .mapZIOPar(8)(process)      // at most 8 effects in flight
    .buffer(16)                 // bounded decoupling; unbounded() is a choice
    .foreach(sink)              // pulling paces the whole pipeline

// hot hand-off: Queue.bounded[Frame](64)  -> offer blocks when full
pitfalls: buffer(16) only decouples while it is bounded; the unbounded() form is a queue in disguise and defeats the purpose.
Queue.unbounded / ZQueue without a capacity in a hot path accumulates until the process dies.
Backpressure does not cross into blocking Java APIs: wrap them in effectBlocking (or a bounded executor) or they will hold a fiber's carrier thread.
A forked producer that ignores interruption cannot be slowed down by a downstream that stops pulling; failure/cancellation must be modelled with the scope.
